content: Non-invasive glucose monitoring refers to the process of measuring blood glucose levels without the need to draw blood, puncture the skin, or cause any pain or trauma. This method is particularly important for individuals with diabetes, as it allows them to monitor their glucose levels to prevent both chronic and acute complications associated with the disease. The pursuit of a successful non-invasive glucose monitoring technique began around 1975 and has continued to this day. Despite decades of research, no clinically or commercially viable product has yet been developed. Over the years, hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested in companies attempting to solve this persistent challenge. However, the journey has been fraught with false starts, premature claims of success, and, in some cases, outright deception by certain investigators. Nevertheless, the majority of researchers in this field have been genuinely motivated by the desire to help individuals with diabetes find a less painful and more convenient way to measure their blood glucose levels. Various approaches have been explored in the quest for non-invasive glucose monitoring. These include near-infrared spectroscopy, which involves measuring glucose levels through the skin using light with wavelengths slightly longer than those in the visible spectrum. Another method, transdermal measurement, attempts to extract glucose through the skin using chemicals, electricity, or ultrasound. Additionally, researchers have investigated measuring the degree to which polarized light is rotated by glucose in the aqueous humor of the eye's anterior chamber. Numerous other techniques have also been tested. A comprehensive list of companies working toward the development of non-invasive glucose monitoring technologies is maintained on a website by a long-time writer who has diabetes.
